# Turin Concrete Map: Sites for a Personal Map of Brutalist Ruins, Quirky History and Thinkers' Seats (Greater Turin, October 2026)

Greater Turin's strongest unusual sites are two pieces of Pier Luigi Nervi engineering, one abandoned and one being revived: the derelict Palazzo del Lavoro, which you can see only from outside, and the Torino Esposizioni hall, which reopens as the city's central library on 11 December 2026. Next come the 2006 Olympic ruins at Cesana Pariol and Pragelato. The bobsleigh track is funded for demolition, so see it soon. For B and C, the best finds are small and close together. Nietzsche's plaque at Via Carlo Alberto 6 is a few doors from Palazzo Campana, the only public building still named after a partisan formation. Cavour's marked table at Del Cambio and Pavese's Caffè Elena are both well documented. Several famous café claims (Gramsci at Caffè San Carlo, Nietzsche "everywhere") rest on tradition, not evidence.

## TL;DR
- **A (main focus):** Palazzo del Lavoro (abandoned, exterior only, future stalled) and Cesana Pariol bob track (still standing as of July 2026, €9M demolition funded) are the two must-sees. Add Ivrea's Talponia, the Torino Esposizioni/Nervi library (opens 11 Dec 2026), Lingotto's rooftop track, Pragelato's ski jumps and the Cimitero Parco.
- **B:** Best quick stops are the Nietzsche plaque (Via Carlo Alberto 6), the 1706/1799 cannonballs set into façades, the Palazzo Campana partisan name, the Fetta di Polenta (54 cm-wide end) and the Mulassano tramezzino plaque.
- **C:** Strongest documented seats are Del Cambio (Cavour's table, with plaque) and Caffè Elena (Pavese, endorsed by the Comune). Fiorio and Al Bicerin rest on long tradition. Caffè Platti has just changed hands and reopens to the public on 23 Oct 2026, according to ANSA and Platti's own site. Libreria Luxemburg has moved, so its historic room is gone.

## How to read the ratings
Each site gets **(a) interest** and **(b) presence** on a 1–5 scale. Presence 5 means a huge physical object; 1 means a plaque or just a spot. Coordinates are approximate (to ~100 m) and should be checked on a map before pinning. "Unverified" means I could not confirm it from a source in this pass.

---

## Category A — Brutalist, concrete and abandoned

### A1. Palazzo del Lavoro (Nervi & Ponti, 1961) — ABANDONED
- **Address / coords:** Via Ventimiglia 201 / Corso Unità d'Italia, Nizza Millefonti (Italia '61 zone). About 45.024, 7.665.
- **What you see:** A giant square hall roofed by 16 freestanding concrete "mushroom" columns with steel umbrella caps. The glass and metal façades are rusting and broken. It is the southern gateway to the city.
- **History:** Nervi won the 1959 competition and built it with his son Antonio and Gino Covre (steel), with Gio Ponti, for Italia '61, the centenary of Unification. It housed Ponti's exhibition "L'uomo al lavoro". A monorail once linked it to the Palazzo delle Mostre. Later it held a university faculty (to 2008), then sporadic discos and events, then nothing. It is listed by the Soprintendenza.
- **Status:** Owned by CDP Immobiliare since 2020. Safety works were completed in early 2025. A shopping-centre plan was dropped. A rumoured Qatari cultural investment (Al Mayassa Al-Thani, ~€500M) reached "stallo" by April 2026. Speaking on TORadio (Torino Oggi, 7 Apr 2026), Mayor Lo Russo blamed the war: "Questa guerra in Iran scatenata da Trump sta producendo danni incalcolabili… per attrarre investitori". In Torino Oggi on 3 Apr 2026, urbanism assessor Mazzoleni said he had not taken anyone to see the building and knew of no concrete talks with Qatar. A 10 Oct 2026 op-ed (Lo Spiffero) says media report it "will not" be restored after all. **Fenced. Do not enter. View from Corso Unità d'Italia and Via Ventimiglia.**
- **Ratings:** Interest 5 / Presence 5.

### A2. Torino Esposizioni — Nervi's Salone B / Padiglione Agnelli (now Biblioteca Civica Centrale)
- **Address / coords:** Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 15–17, edge of Parco del Valentino. About 45.054, 7.685.
- **What you see:** Nervi's 1948–50 prefabricated ferrocement vault, the "cattedrale moderna", plus Morandi's 1959 underground hall. It has been restored by Rafael Moneo with Isolarchitetti. New functions sit mostly in a hypogeum, so the great hall stays open.
- **History:** The complex was built by Ettore Sottsass Sr. in 1938, bombed, and rebuilt by Nervi as an exhibition hall. It hosted early editions of the Salone del Libro. The restoration is a ~€166M PNRR project. The Comune di Torino (1 Jul 2026) gives "una superficie complessiva di 20mila metri quadrati", which would make it among the largest public libraries in Italy and the EU. Culture assessor Rosanna Purchia gave a different figure in Jan 2026: 24,000 m², with 1,000 study seats and 150,000 open-shelf items (Quotidiano Piemontese).
- **Status:** Opening date repeatedly slipped (30 June 2026, then "autumn"). Presenting "Vale", the new Valentino cultural hub, Mayor Lo Russo announced **11 December 2026** as the public opening, with programming starting in November (Exibart). **Not open on 20 Oct 2026.** Expected to be free, as a public library.
- **Ratings:** Interest 5 / Presence 5 (once open).

### A3. Cesana Pariol bobsleigh/luge track (Torino 2006) — ABANDONED, DEMOLITION PENDING
- **Address / coords:** Località Pariol, Cesana Torinese (upper Val di Susa), about 85 km from Turin. About 44.95, 6.80 (unverified, check on a map).
- **What you see:** A long zig-zag "serpentone" of concrete and sheet metal down a larch slope, with refrigeration plant and stands. It is the nearest thing in Italy to Sarajevo's Trebević track.
- **History:** Cost €110M and seated 7,130 spectators. Armin Zöggeler never lost on it and won one of Italy's five Turin golds there. Running losses were about €1.3–1.5M a year, and it closed in 2011/2012 (sources differ). In 2023 Italy floated reviving it for Milano-Cortina 2026, and the IOC rejected the idea ("already abandoned once").
- **Status:** €9M has been allocated for (partial) demolition and "rinaturalizzazione". Government commissioner Vincenzo Coccolo told the post-Olympic press conference with Minister Abodi (Eco del Chisone, 30 Apr 2025): "I cantieri saranno aperti nell'estate 2026, sia per Cesana e sia per Pragelato". Earlier reports expected about a year of works. **As of July 2026 it was still standing.** I found no report confirming that work has started this autumn. Expect fencing. It may be partly gone or a building site when you arrive, so check local news (Luna Nuova, ValsusaOggi) before the trip.
- **Ratings:** Interest 5 / Presence 5 (falling).

### A4. Pragelato Olympic ski jumps (Stadio del Trampolino)
- **Address / coords:** Pragelato, Val Chisone. About 45.01, 6.94 (unverified).
- **What you see:** Five jumps (HS106 and HS140 Olympic hills), a judges' tower and an abandoned hotel at the foot. The jumps' green plastic summer matting is disintegrating, and one 2025 visitor called it an ecological "time bomb".
- **History:** Cost about €34M. Later "tubing" and summer jumping were tried and failed. The Olympic hills are not owned by the comune.
- **Status:** The area below the jumps is being converted for biathlon and roller-skiing (≈€5M, Universiade works, permanent facility targeted for winter 2026–27). **The jumps themselves are being kept, not demolished** ("troppo caro smontarli"). Expect active building sites below them.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 5.

### A5. Ivrea — Talponia (Unità Residenziale Ovest) and Hotel La Serra (Unità Residenziale Est)
- **Address / coords:** Talponia is about 45.4591, 7.8673. La Serra is on Corso Botta, about 45.4664, 7.8797. Ivrea is about 1 hr from Turin by train.
- **What you see:** Talponia is a semicircular, half-buried "horizontal skyscraper" about 300 m long, with 82 duplex and simplex cells facing a hillside under a grass roof. La Serra, by Cappai & Mainardis (1968–70s), is a sculptural concrete hotel and cultural block in the town centre. Roman remains were found during its excavation.
- **History:** Talponia was commissioned by Olivetti in Sept 1968 from Gabetti & Isola, completed in late 1970, and housed visiting staff. It is part of the UNESCO site "Ivrea, Industrial City of the 20th Century" (2018).
- **Status:** Talponia is lived in, so walk past respectfully. One flat is now the private **Casa Museo olivettiana** (curated by Giovanna Faso); check its visiting terms. A new UNESCO **Visitor Centre** opened on 12 Sept 2026, with weekend guided tours at 10:00 and 15:00. Autumn 2026 "Welcome Tours" run about 2.5 hrs.
- **Ratings:** Interest 5 / Presence 4.

### A6. Lingotto and the Pista 500 rooftop test track
- **Address / coords:** Via Nizza 230/262 (Pinacoteca Agnelli entrance inside the Lingotto centre). About 45.032, 7.665.
- **What you see:** The 1920s Fiat factory's rooftop banked test track, 28 m up. It is now a planted art garden (about 6,000 m², about 40,000 plants), with Renzo Piano's "Bolla" and "Scrigno" additions.
- **History:** Cars were built floor by floor going up and tested on the roof. It is a key monument of Italian concrete industrial architecture.
- **Status:** Pinacoteca Agnelli is open Tue–Sun 10:00–19:00 (schedule valid 21 Sept–28 Oct 2026). Per Turismo Torino (the official tourist board), the Pinacoteca + Pista 500 combo costs €12 full / €8 reduced, and the Pista 500 alone €4 full / €2 reduced. Note that the site sometimes closes early for private events. It is a tourist icon, so it is lower priority, but it is pure "odd modernist infrastructure".
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 5.

### A7. Chiesa del Santo Volto (Mario Botta, 2004–06) and Parco Dora industrial skeletons
- **Address / coords:** Via Val della Torre 11. About 45.087, 7.663. Parco Dora is adjacent (Spina 3).
- **What you see:** A seven-tower brick church on a former Fiat Ferriere steelworks site. The roughly 60 m steelworks chimney is kept as a "campanile" wrapped in a steel helix with a cross on top, and the bells actually sit at its base. Next door, Parco Dora keeps steel skeletons of the old sheds and former cooling and washing tanks.
- **History:** The first church built in Turin in the 21st century and now the city's co-cathedral. It sits on the "città del lavoro" site, and the chimney was kept as a memory of the workers.
- **Status:** Active parish, free, open around services. The park is public.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 5.

### A8. Cimitero Parco (1972) — landscape cemetery
- **Address / coords:** Via Agostino Bertani 80 (end of Corso Orbassano, Gerbido). About 45.03, 7.60 (unverified).
- **What you see:** About 690,000 m² of rolling lawns. Artificial hillocks hide the concrete burial complexes, and simple slabs lie flush in the grass with the Alps behind. There are Islamic, Evangelical and Romanian Orthodox sections, including an Orthodox chapel.
- **History:** Built 1969–72 when the Monumentale was full during the Fiat-migration boom. It deliberately follows Nordic "park cemetery" models, described as "egalitarian modernism".
- **Status:** Municipal cemetery, free. Check opening hours on the comune site.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 4.

### A9. Rifugio antiaereo di Piazza Risorgimento (WWII public shelter)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Risorgimento (entrance between Via Nicola Fabrizi and Via Buronzo). About 45.077, 7.656.
- **What you see:** Three parallel reinforced-concrete galleries about 40 m long and 4.5 m wide, 12 m underground, with 80 cm walls. Wartime rules of conduct are still painted on the walls. The access turrets have murals by XEL.
- **History:** One of about 45 public shelters built 1942–44. Turin suffered bombing from 12 June 1940 to 5 April 1945, with 2,069 dead.
- **Status:** **Only on special openings.** These include Museo Diffuso della Resistenza tours, FAI days and Monumenti Aperti (one edition ran Sat–Sun 10–12 and 14:30–16). Book through the Museo Diffuso (011 01120780). The shelter under **Palazzo Civico** offers free guided visits on the 4th Tuesday of each month for groups and schools, booked via the Cerimoniale office.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 4.

### A10. Corso Taranto IACP housing (late 1960s)
- **Address / coords:** Corso Taranto / Via Cravero area, Barriera di Milano / Regio Parco. About 45.095, 7.708 (unverified).
- **What you see:** Sixteen eight-storey heavy-prefab slabs (652 flats) lined up on the heliothermic axis, designed by Nello Renacco. These are Turin's nearest analogue to a Falowiec or Aillaud estate in spirit, though not in scale.
- **History:** Built for southern migrants drawn by Fiat. Its tenants' committee is one of Turin's oldest, celebrating 50 years in 2017. It is the subject of the book *Abitare i margini* (2020) on 1970s housing struggles.
- **Status:** Lived-in social housing. Exterior only.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 4.

### A11. Chiesa del Gesù Redentore (Nicola & Leonardo Mosso, 1955–57)
- **Address / coords:** Mirafiori Nord, Borgo Cina, Piazza Giovanni XXIII (address unverified). About 45.035, 7.627 (unverified).
- **What you see:** Bare brick walls under a faceted exposed reinforced-concrete vault, with a single nave.
- **History:** Considered Nicola Mosso's key religious work, with interest "beyond local" significance. Leonardo Mosso was later a well-known Alvar Aalto collaborator.
- **Status:** Active parish. The roof was restored in 2002.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 3.

### A12. Torre BBPR (Reale Mutua tower)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Statuto / Corso Francia corner. About 45.077, 7.670.
- **What you see:** A brick-clad "post-rationalist/brutalist" tower with oriel bays and porticoes, Milan-school neo-liberty. It is Turin's cousin of the Torre Velasca.
- **History:** Built for Reale Mutua by BBPR. Dates conflict: 1955–59 (it.wikipedia) vs 1959–61 (SugoNews).
- **Status:** Offices. Exterior only.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 4.

### A13. Minor or lower-confidence A sites
- **Villa Gontero, Cumiana** (Carlo Graffi with Sergio Musmeci, 1969–71). Exposed concrete, Vibrapac blocks and orange accents. **Private house; I could not verify any access.** Interest 3 / Presence 2.
- **DUPARC Contemporary Suites** (1969–71 concrete building, now an art hotel with a Richard Woods installation in the column-lined lobby). The address is not verified here, so check it. Interest 2 / Presence 3.
- **Ex SNOS / Officine Savigliano, Corso Mortara.** Listed among Italian brutalist works by it.wikipedia, but I did not verify its current state. Interest 3 / Presence 3 (unverified).

## Category B — Quirky historical pass-by sights

### B1. Nietzsche's lodging plaque and the "Turin horse" square
- **Address / coords:** Via Carlo Alberto 6, facing Piazza Carlo Alberto. About 45.0688, 7.6857.
- **What you see:** A marble plaque on the façade. His room was the fifth window from the corner, on the 4th floor, above the Galleria Subalpina entrance.
- **History:** He stayed from 21 Sept 1888 to 9 Jan 1889, paying 30 lire a month to the newsagent Davide Fino, and wrote *Ecce Homo* and finished *Twilight of the Idols* here. On 3 Jan 1889 he collapsed in the street. **The horse-hugging story is disputed:** most sources place it in Piazza Carlo Alberto, one regional tourism page says Piazza San Carlo, and several call it "more legendary than true". It inspired Béla Tarr's film *The Turin Horse*.
- **Status:** Street plaque, always visible. The flat is private.
- **Ratings:** Interest 5 / Presence 1.

### B2. Palazzo Campana — the partisan-named university building
- **Address / coords:** Via Carlo Alberto 10 (a few doors from B1). About 45.0683, 7.6857.
- **What you see:** A grand palazzo with a university entrance.
- **History:** The former Fascist "Casa del Littorio". Brigate Nere held arrested partisans here, and their graffiti stayed visible for years. After 1945 it became a university building and took the name of the fallen partisan Campana. According to Istoreto, it is the only public building in the city to keep a partisan name. In 1967–68 it was the epicentre of Turin's student occupation (general knowledge; not verified here).
- **Status:** University building. The courtyard is usually accessible in term time.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 3.

### B3. Cannonballs embedded in façades (sieges of 1706 and 1799)
- **Address / coords:** The courtyard of Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana, Via della Consolata 1 bis, has two balls on its north façade. A shell is walled into the building north of the start of Via Palazzo di Città, on Piazza Palazzo di Città. About 45.075, 7.680 and 45.073, 7.683.
- **What you see:** Black iron spheres set into plaster.
- **History:** Projectiles from the French siege of 1706 were deliberately walled in as memorials. Later shots fired in 1799 by the French garrison holding the Cittadella against Suvorov's Austro-Russians were also preserved.
- **Status:** Public façades. Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana's courtyard is reachable during business hours.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 2.

### B4. Fetta di Polenta (Casa Scaccabarozzi, Alessandro Antonelli)
- **Address / coords:** Corner of Corso San Maurizio and Via Giulia di Barolo (address from general knowledge, unverified). About 45.071, 7.695.
- **What you see:** A many-storey wedge-shaped house whose narrow end is **54 cm** wide. Built by the Mole's architect.
- **Status:** Private building, view from the street.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 3.

### B5. Caffè Mulassano — the tramezzino's birthplace (plaque)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Castello 15. About 45.0705, 7.6845.
- **What you see:** A 31 m² Liberty-style café, a Locale Storico d'Italia since 1985. Inside, a plaque reads "Nel 1926, la signora Angela Demichelis Nebiolo, inventò il tramezzino". The name is attributed to D'Annunzio, and sources give 1925 or 1926.
- **Status:** Open, roughly 09:30–20:00 (to 19:30 Tue/Wed per TripAdvisor). It is classed as B (a "first"), not C.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 2.

### B6. Palazzo Carignano — first Italian Parliament (icon, deprioritised)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Carignano / Via Accademia delle Scienze 5. About 45.0695, 7.6855.
- **What you see:** Guarini's undulating brick baroque façade. Behind it is the 1861 hall where the first Italian Parliament proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy, now the Museo del Risorgimento (general knowledge; check current hours and price on the museum site).
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 4.

### B7. Piazza San Carlo crowd-crush memorial plaque (3 June 2017)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza San Carlo. About 45.0677, 7.6827.
- **What you see / history:** A plaque placed in 2019 for the victims of the panic during the Juventus Champions League final screening, which was triggered by a robbery gang using pepper spray. Three people eventually died. Four convictions for manslaughter followed.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 1.

### B8. "Baci Urbani" — the palazzo with a piercing
- **Address / coords:** Piazzetta Corpus Domini 19, corner of the 4th floor. About 45.0735, 7.6825.
- **What you see:** An oversized metal "piercing" ring stuck into the corner of an 18th-century building. It was meant as a temporary art installation and never removed.
- **Ratings:** Interest 2 / Presence 1.

### B9. Insurrection of 26–28 April 1945 — street plaques (lower confidence)
- **What / where:** Istoreto's "Che il silenzio non sia silenzio" catalogue records hundreds of plaques for people killed during the liberation. One record: a nine-year-old boy shot by a fascist sniper on 27 April 1945 in front of **Via Madama Cristina 137** while picking up insurrection leaflets. I could not confirm a plaque at that exact spot. Separately, on 30 April 1945 retreating Germans massacred **67 people at Grugliasco**, including the salesian partisan chaplain Mario Caustico; a memorial exists in Grugliasco, but its exact location was not verified here.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 1 (unverified spots).

### B10. Searched but not confirmed as visitable
- **Standard measures (piede liprando):** In 1798 the Accademia delle Scienze had official standard samples of Piedmontese units made by G. Matthey. **I found no public outdoor standard-measure markers in Turin** like the Paris mètre étalon. Treat this as a lead to check, not a site.
- **Visible WWII bullet or shrapnel scars:** I found no sourced, specific façade location. Don't pin one without on-site confirmation.

## Category C — Places to sit where thinkers sat

### C1. Ristorante Del Cambio (since 1757) — Cavour's table
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Carignano 2. About 45.0697, 7.6858.
- **Link (documented):** Regional tourism site Piemonteitalia: "Nella sala più ampia è conservato il tavolo dove sedeva abitualmente il Conte Camillo Benso di Cavour". Rolling Stone Italia: "Il suo tavolo è ancora segnato con una targa commemorativa". From it he could watch Palazzo Carignano, the parliament. The longer celebrity lists (Casanova, Puccini, Balzac, Nietzsche, Verdi) are **promotional and unverified.**
- **Status:** Open, Michelin one star. Dinner roughly 19:30–23:30, Sunday lunch, plus a bistro at lunch. You can ask for Cavour's table when booking. Expensive; check delcambio.it.
- **Ratings:** Interest 5 / Presence 4.

### C2. Caffè Elena — Pavese's café
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Vittorio Veneto 5/b. About 45.0650, 7.6930.
- **Link (well supported):** Comune di Torino: "oggi si può fare colazione dove Cesare Pavese trascorreva il proprio tempo a scrivere". The original red breccia-marble tables survive. Giuseppe Carpano is said to have perfected his vermouth here in 1889–1902. A blog claim that Nietzsche "certainly" went is **unsupported.**
- **Status:** Open. Mon–Fri 08–00, closed Wednesday; Sat 09–01; Sun 09–00 (official site).
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 3.

### C3. Caffè Fiorio (1780) — Cavour's Whist Club, "café of the Machiavellis and pigtails"
- **Address / coords:** Via Po 8. About 45.0702, 7.6830.
- **Link (tradition, popular sources):** Frequented by Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo, Santorre di Santarosa and Cavour, who is said to have founded the Whist Club here. Carlo Alberto supposedly asked "What do they say at Fiorio?" It was the conservative café, in contrast to San Carlo. The Nietzsche link, through its ice cream, is plausible but comes only from popular sources.
- **Status:** No closure reported. Check hours. Ignore one guide's wrong address (Piazza Castello 29).
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 3.

### C4. Al Bicerin (1763)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza della Consolata 5. About 45.0767, 7.6800.
- **Link:** By long tradition, Cavour drank here while waiting for the royal family to leave the Consolata sanctuary; one source frames it as "legend has it". Names on the wall (Dumas, Puccini, Nietzsche, Gozzano, Calvino) are tradition. The firmest literary tie is fictional: **Umberto Eco set a scene of *The Prague Cemetery* here.**
- **Status:** Open, **closed Wednesdays**. About 08:30–19:30 (sources vary). Tiny, so expect a queue.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 3.

### C5. Caffè San Carlo (1822)
- **Address / coords:** Piazza San Carlo 156. About 45.0675, 7.6825.
- **Link:** A Risorgimento patriots' café (D'Azeglio, Cavour, Rattazzi, Giolitti, Crispi), closed several times for suspected subversion. A 1920s literary circle met here. In 1899 the Duke of the Abruzzi reportedly planned his polar expedition here (sources say "Antarctic", but the Stella Polare voyage went to the Arctic). **The Gramsci/"Ordine Nuovo was conceived here" claim is a stock marketing phrase.** One source hedges it with "pare", and there is no scholarly source.
- **Status:** Open, roughly 08:00–00:00. Management has changed several times, and it was closed for restoration 1953–63.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 3.

### C6. Caffè Platti (1870/1875) — Pavese, Luigi Einaudi
- **Address / coords:** Corso Vittorio Emanuele II 72. About 45.0640, 7.6760.
- **Link:** Popular sources: Luigi Einaudi, Cesare Pavese, Natalia Ginzburg, and the founders of Fiat and Lavazza.
- **Status:** **Changed owner in Sept 2026.** Gerla 1927 sold it to Villa Cimena Luxury Events (Balma family) through a new company, Platti il Salotto del Gusto S.r.l. Closed from about 1 Oct 2026 for restyling. ANSA (1 Oct 2026): "L'inaugurazione su invito è prevista per il 22 ottobre, mentre dal 23 ottobre Caffè Platti tornerà ad accogliere il pubblico". Platti's own website says "CI RIVEDIAMO IL 23 OTTOBRE". It also went bankrupt and closed in 2015 before reopening.
- **Ratings:** Interest 3 / Presence 3.

### C7. Biblioteca Reale (Royal Library) — Musei Reali
- **Address / coords:** Piazza Castello 191. About 45.0720, 7.6855.
- **What / link:** Founded by Carlo Alberto (1831–37), with Pelagio Palagi's vaulted Salone. It holds Leonardo's drawings, including the self-portrait. **I found no sourced list of famous readers**, so this is a "sit in a great reading room" pick, not a "sat where X sat" one.
- **Status (from 1 Jun 2026):** Tourists see the Salone with a Musei Reali ticket, Mon and Fri 9:00–13:30 and Tue, Thu and Sat 13:30–18:30; currently it also hosts "Margherita, prima Regina d'Italia" until 6 Jan 2027. The **reading room is for adult scholars only**: email booking at least 24 hrs ahead, Mon and Fri 13:30–18:30, Tue, Thu and Sat 8:30–13:30, closed Wednesday.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 4.

### C8. Library of the Accademia delle Scienze (1783)
- **Address / coords:** Entrance Via Maria Vittoria 3 (palace at Via Accademia delle Scienze 6). About 45.0690, 7.6850.
- **Link:** Lagrange was a founder. Early members included Monge, Laplace, d'Alembert and Euler. It holds Coronelli globes.
- **Status:** "Esclusivamente su appuntamento", Mon–Thu 9–13 and 15–17, Fri 9–13, through a form. Casual visitors usually get in only during events or conferences.
- **Ratings:** Interest 4 / Presence 3.

### C9. Lower-confidence cafés (popular sources only)
- **Caffè Torino** (Piazza San Carlo, 1903): Pavese, Einaudi and De Gasperi per a café blog. Interest 2 / Presence 3.
- **Pfatisch** (Via Sacchi): the Savoy princes, Pavese, Primo Levi, Montanelli, Soldati and Bobbio per a food blog. Unverified. Interest 3 / Presence 3.
- **Stratta** (Piazza San Carlo): Cavour's famous order of 29 kg of marrons glacés and more (2,547.60 lire). It is a pastry shop rather than a sit-down café. Interest 3 / Presence 2.

### C — Rejected / closed / myth list
- **Libreria Luxemburg, Via Accademia delle Scienze 3:** **Gone from that site.** It closed on 6 Jan 2025 and reopened on 20 Jan 2025 at Via Cesare Battisti 7–11, with an entrance from Galleria Subalpina and a Baratti & Milano corner. The 1872 shop (founded as Libreria Casanova; under Angelo Pezzana from the 1970s) survives as a business, but the historic room is lost. Visit only as a good bookshop.
- **Nietzsche's flat (Via Carlo Alberto 6):** This is a house, so it is excluded by your rules; the plaque is mapped as B1.
- **"Gramsci founded Ordine Nuovo at Caffè San Carlo":** Marketing or tradition only; *L'Ordine Nuovo* was founded 1 May 1919 by Gramsci, Togliatti, Tasca and Terracini.
- **"Gobetti and Gramsci debating in a café in the 1930s"** (Pannunzio Magazine): **Chronologically impossible.** Gobetti died in 1926, and Gramsci was imprisoned from 1926.
- **Nietzsche "regular" at Al Bicerin / Caffè Elena:** Unsourced. The Fiorio link is the least weak.

# Turin Concrete Map — Category A, Second Pass (27 Oct 2026)

The strongest new finds for your taste are Gabetti & Isola's factory-shed church at Piossasco, Mollino's Teatro Regio (bookable backstage tours) and Lago Nero sled station, the Italia '61 monorail stumps plus a "beam graveyard" in Nichelino, the Collegno asylum park, the Orco-valley dams, and a little-known Morandi–Niemeyer headquarters at Pianezza. Around them sit a dense layer of periferia housing, churches and fenced industrial carcasses. This pass adds 40 new sites, grouped by type. Several are time-sensitive: the Trincerone becomes a Metro 2 construction site in the first half of 2027, and the alpine forts and dam roads are mostly seasonal and already closed for winter.

## TL;DR
- **Best new urban sites:** Teatro Regio (guided tours €10, Sat 15:00/16:30 and Sun 11:00, Italian only), the Italia '61 monorail remnants, Torri Pitagora and Casa dell'Obelisco (Jaretti & Luzi), the Falchera and Vallette estates, and a cluster of post-conciliar concrete churches (Santi Apostoli in Piossasco, San Paolo Apostolo, San Pietro in Vincoli in Moriondo).
- **Best day trips:** Ivrea beyond Talponia (new UNESCO Visitor Centre at Via Jervis 11, free, Tue–Sun 10–18 until 15 Nov 2026), the Ceresole/Serrù dam system in the Orco valley, Fenestrelle (guided-only, booking required), and Mollino's Chalet at Lago Nero above Sauze d'Oulx.
- **Act soon or skip:** the Trincerone (Metro 2 tender published in the EU Official Journal on 11 May 2026; Torino Cronaca says first-section sites start in the first half of 2027) and the ex-Borsa Valori (closed since 1992; Torino Oggi says the building site may open in 2028 with completion in 2030; exterior only). Exilles and the high Orco roads are closed for winter, and several abandoned factories are fenced and exterior-only.

## Key Findings
- **Mollino is under-mined in the first pass.** Three buildings are accessible: the Teatro Regio (tours), Palazzo degli Affari (public offices, works due to finish mid-October 2026) and the Lago Nero sled station (a working ski-slope refuge). Together they form a strong single-architect thread.
- **The churches are the richest seam.** Turin's post-conciliar building boom under Cardinal Pellegrino (1965–77) produced a factory-shed church (Piossasco), a floating-roof concrete centre plan (San Paolo Apostolo), and Mosso and Mosso-derived exposed-beam roofs (Moriondo, Nichelino). The Diocese of Turin catalogue and Carla Zito's *Casa tra le case* (Effatà 2013) list many more.
- **Italia '61 has three separate remnants, not one:** the 14 surviving spans out of 58 at the lake, the north station (now Casa UGI), and the dismantled beams lying in a Nichelino field (reported 2019; current state unverified).
- **The hidden "Niemeyer in Turin":** the FATA headquarters at Pianezza (1976–77), by Riccardo Morandi with Oscar Niemeyer and Massimo Gennari, is listed by Treccani. Its current state and use could not be verified, so treat it as a scouting target, exterior only.
- **Industrial ruins are almost all fenced.** OSI-Ghia, the ThyssenKrupp/Teksid belt and the ex-Superga are exterior-only. Torino Oggi (20 Jul 2026) reports that the City will sign a public-private partnership with Paratissima to turn ex-Superga into a culture hub, a €3.5 m investment with about three years of works.

# Turin Concrete Map — Third Pass, Category A: Verification, Gap-Fill and New Ground

The strongest result of this pass is that the FATA headquarters in Pianezza, by Oscar Niemeyer and Riccardo Morandi, is real, still in company use at Via dei Prati 2, and worth a dedicated stop: a 100-metre "land bridge" with 21.30 m cantilevers, seen from the street. Most other Job 1 leads resolve to "map as pass-by" or "skip". The Italia '61 monorail beam graveyard is real but can only be seen from the motorway, and its 2026 state is unconfirmed. The Circarama is entirely gone. Officine Grandi Motori is a fenced demolition site. The ex Mercato dei Fiori reopened in October 2025 as a gym. Job 2 and Job 3 produced 17 new sites, fewer than the 25–45 target. The ceiling came from thin online sourcing for Turin's post-conciliar churches (the Diocese catalogue PDF blocks automated access), not from a lack of places. The church section therefore mixes confirmed sites with flagged "eyeball it" leads.

### Notes on Job 1

**FATA headquarters, Pianezza.** The MiC Censimento delle architetture italiane dal 1945 lists it as "Uffici FATA (Fabbrica Automazione Trasporti e Affini) Engineering", with Niemeyer as architect and Morandi as structural engineer. It describes the building's "strabiliante effetto di sospensione" (astonishing effect of suspension), which makes it read like "un vero e proprio ponte di terraferma" (a true land bridge). The side cantilevers are 21.30 m and the spans between piers 32.40 m. The load comes down onto six hollow piers of 1.50 × 3.60 m, joined by a hollow prestressed-concrete beam. The intermediate floors hang from the great arches on bolted steel ties. In lineage it is the Turin sibling of Niemeyer's Mondadori HQ at Segrate. Dates conflict: Structurae gives 1976–77, while Marzia Marandola's Casabella 764 (2008) article gives 1976–79. Treat 1976 as design and 1979 as completion. Domus covered it in 1977 and 1980. Structurae lists it as "in use", and the company still trades from Via dei Prati 2. It is private offices: photograph it from the road and do not enter the grounds. For someone who loved Niemeyer in Paris, this is the single most important new pin on the map. Rating: 4/5 general interest, 4/5 physical presence.

**Monorail beam graveyard.** TorinoStoria first published this on 29 Dec 2015 ("Ritrovato a Nichelino il cimitero della storica monorotaia"). It reported twenty prestressed-concrete Alweg beams lying in a field near the Nichelino Sud service area and the Via Napoli overpass. Il Torinese repeated it in Jan 2019, quoting engineer Luca Valzano: hollow-section beams 1.4 m deep, about 20 m long and about 40 t each. The volunteer association Amici di Italia '61 puts the beams on the Tangenziale *Nord* direction Rivoli, on the right, about 100 m after the "Nichelino Nord" service area. That conflicts with "Sud" in the press reports, so treat the exact spot as uncertain. The same association reports more beams at Collegno, lying on the former TTS rail siding at Tamagnone just past the station, and others possibly dumped in the Dora. Ten more were found in 1994 in an illegal dump at Parco del Meisino. No source confirms the beams are still in place in 2026, and none establishes who owns the land. You cannot stop on the Tangenziale. Verdict: a moving glimpse at most; don't send anyone into the field.

**The five churches.** Sources confirm architects, dates and addresses, but none online confirms *exposed* concrete for these five.
- *San Luca Evangelista*, Via Celeste Negarville 14. By prof. arch. Mario Federico Roggero. MuseoTorino dates it 1967–71; the Diocese catalogue says 1967–70. It was built in "una zona caratterizzata da una forte concentrazione di case popolari" (an area with a heavy concentration of public housing), in the Mirafiori Sud estates. It is also a MITO SettembreMusica concert venue. Mass is Saturday 18:15 and Sunday 9:30/11:00/18:15 (Diocese listing). Worth pairing with the Mirafiori Sud estates. Provisional 3/5, 3/5.
- *Gesù Operaio*, Via Leoncavallo 18, Barriera di Milano. Ing. Felice Bardelli designed it, and MuseoTorino notes he co-designed Palazzo Nuovo. Built 1963–67 and consecrated by Cardinal Pellegrino on 26 Nov 1967. It has a basketball and volleyball gym in the undercroft, and CEI's census flags the "impianto strutturale" (structural system) as a notable feature. It is the closest family relative of a building already on the map. Provisional 3/5, 3/5.
- *Santa Maria Goretti*, Via Actis 18–20, Parella. Architects Pasquale Carbonara and Michele Berardo, built by Impresa Giacomo Broglino. The parish says it was built in 1965 (catalogue: 1964–67) and consecrated on 16 Oct 1966. It is modest: the parish's own 1960s blessing text describes it as "di modeste proporzioni" (of modest proportions), and the earlier chapel was 320 m². Pass-by, 2/5.
- *"Madonna del Carmine"* is not in Turin. The catalogue entry is "Sacro Cuore di Gesù e Madonna del Carmine, Via Rivodora 7", Unità Pastorale 29 – San Mauro Torinese, by Ing. Augusto Vaudetti with Rocchietti, 1964–65. Don't confuse it with Juvarra's baroque Carmine in Via del Carmine. Low priority.
- *Beata Vergine Consolata*, Roggero, 1965, appears under Unità Pastorale 32 – Lanzo. The town and address are unconfirmed. Unresolved.

**Officine Grandi Motori.** According to ANSA (19 Feb 2025), the complex "si estende per circa 70.000 metri quadrati", with "progressiva dismissione dal 1971", and names Impresa Mattioda as the "soggetto attuatore" (developer) of the redevelopment. The Città di Torino approved the planning variant unanimously in January 2023. Demolitions began in February 2025 under contractor Perino Piero srl, starting with the southern lot. In January 2026 (Torino Oggi, 12 Jan 2026), replying to an interpellanza by councillor Pierlucio Firrao (Torino Bellissima), the planning councillor (assessore all'Urbanistica) Paolo Mazzoleni said demolitions were only partly complete, that "necessari controlli sulla staticità delle strutture" (structural-stability checks) were slowing work, and that Esselunga had been granted an extension to 30 March 2026 to file the definitive clean-up plan for its portion. The plan keeps the 1911 "Basilica" by Giacomo Mattè Trucco for non-food retail with a public car park, and turns the "Lingottino" on Corso Vercelli/Corso Vigevano into student housing for 250–300 beds. A 15,000 m² garden is planned, plus an Esselunga logistics hub. Squatting was reported during the works. Status: fenced construction site, exterior only. The surviving shells are still dramatic from Corso Vigevano, but the view changes month by month. Rating 3/5, 3/5, time-sensitive.

**Ex Mercato dei Fiori.** The 1960 market hall at Via Perugia 29 was converted into the GOfit sports centre, which opened in October 2025. The city says the conversion was done "nel pieno rispetto dell'architettura originaria" (with full respect for the original architecture). The public garden in front opened on 2 March 2026. It is no longer derelict. Map only if you want the 1960 hall form in the Aurora cluster next to OGM. 1/5, 2/5.

**Circarama.** FIAT built it as a demountable pavilion in steel, aluminium and plastics, 32 m in diameter and 12 m high. It was derelict by 1970–78 (Archivio Storico and Fondazione Gramsci photos). The site at Via Ventimiglia 199 is now the "Il laghetto" nursery. Nothing survives. The Amici di Italia '61 exhibition at Palazzo Lascaris closed on 10 June 2026. Skip.

**SS. Trinità, Nichelino.** The Diocese and the Annuario Cattolico give the parish church as **Via Stupinigi 16, 10042 Nichelino**. The new church ("Chiesa Grande") was built 1970–73 and consecrated on 15 April 1973. It has a concrete frame, exposed brick and large glazed areas, and seats over 600. Other descriptions place it on Piazza della Libertà facing Via S. Francesco d'Assisi. The old church of Santi Matteo e Rocco is the one *on* Piazza della Libertà. **Viale Kennedy 28**, which directory sites list, is the subsidiary church of San Vincenzo de' Paoli, not the Pratesi building. Pin the modern church building next to Piazza della Libertà, and check the exact pin on satellite view.

The best find in Turin for someone who liked the Athens bullet holes is a real bullet mark: a dent from the 21–22 September 1864 massacre on a bas-relief of the Caval ëd Bronz in Piazza San Carlo, next to a 1999 plaque for the victims. Around it is a dense set of small, real-history spots. ## TL;DR
- **Best pick:** the 1864 bullet dent on the Caval ëd Bronz plinth plus the plaque at Piazza San Carlo 161. It is a physical scar from the "first state massacre" of united Italy, and almost nobody notices it.
- **Coverage:** 42 sites, all checkable on foot in minutes. Theme 1 (executions and violence) and the Resistance plaques are rich. Theme 3 (famous deaths and disasters) is solid. Theme 2's painted "R" shelter signs are the weak spot: their survival is documented, but no specific street address could be confirmed.
- **Where to put your time:** the Pietro Micca tunnels (booked visit) and the Superga crash wall are the two "substantial" experiences. Everything else is a plaque, a stone or a gap, so batch them by neighbourhood.

## 1. The Best 10

1. **Caval ëd Bronz bullet dent + 1864 massacre plaque (Piazza San Carlo)**: a bullet mark on the Cateau-Cambrésis bas-relief and a 1999 plaque at no. 161. It is a real scar from the night soldiers fired on Turin's crowd.
2. **Museo Pietro Micca tunnels (Via Guicciardini 7/A)**: you go underground to the stair Micca ran down and the spot where his body was found, 30 August 1706. This is the most physical site on the list.
3. **Superga crash wall**: the rear retaining wall of the basilica, still marked by the 4 May 1949 impact, with the marble plaque listing the Grande Torino victims.
4. **Sacrario del Martinetto (Corso Svizzera / Corso Appio Claudio)**: the surviving small rifle range where RSI firing squads shot around sixty partisans. Counts differ: MuseoTorino's range page says 59, matching the plaque; its Sacrario page says "oltre 60"; ANPI says 61. A stone post and a plaque with 59 names.
5. **Teatro di Torino ruin (Via Verdi 29)**: the perimeter walls of a theatre gutted by bombs in December 1942. MuseoTorino calls it the city's only substantial visible ruin from the bombing.
6. **Paolo Sacchi plaque, Arsenale (Piazza Borgo Dora 49)**: the 1886 bronze plaque on the old arsenal. It honours the sergeant who, per Atlante di Torino, kept 40,000 kg of powder from catching fire on 26 April 1852. The death toll is disputed: Wikipedia's Sacchi page says 26, while its Arsenale page says 20 dead plus 3 who died later in hospital.
7. **Rondò della Forca, Cafasso monument**: a 1960 bronze of the "gallows priest", standing on the spot of the 1835–1853 public gallows. The Atlas description says it was requested by prisoners.
8. **Via Cibrario 1, "in questo luogo il piombo nazifascista…"**: the plaque on the exact spot where nine partisans, two of them unidentified Frenchmen, were shot on 12 October 1944.
9. **Monte dei Cappuccini shelter mouths (Via Gaetano Giardino 9)**: eight WWII tunnel entrances visible in the hillside retaining wall, six of them bricked up. War infrastructure you can read from the pavement.
10. **Piazza XVIII Dicembre plaque (corner of Via Cernaia)**: marks the 18–20 December 1922 Fascist massacre, Italy's first big squadrist killing spree, with a second plaque in the metro station.

- **What you see:** a bronze of Cafasso holding a crucifix out to a condemned man, by Virgilio Audagna, set in a traffic island.
- **History:** public hangings were held here, in open country near the prison, from 1835 to 1852/1853. Earlier they took place in Via Giulio (1821–1834), Piazza delle Erbe and Piazza San Carlo. Cafasso spiritually accompanied 57 condemned men. AtlasFor and Comuni-Italiani say the monument was "voluto dai carcerati d'Italia", and it was put up in 1960/61 "nel punto esatto" of the scaffold.
- **Source conflict:** sources disagree on when hangings ended here. Wikipedia and AtlasFor say 1852/1853. A blog (Il Cinzanino) says 1863, and Cordola says the scaffold stones moved to the Cittadella in 1853, with the last execution in 1864. The name "Rondò della Forca" was never official.
- **Legend:** the "black triangle" and "magic Turin" framing is tourist esoterica. The story that 16-year-old RSI auxiliary Marilena Grill was shot here by partisans in May 1945 comes from a single low-grade wiki source and is unverified.

- **Also here:** the square was the core of the old ghetto. The Istoreto guide notes the building on the corner of Via des Ambrois, which has four floors plus a mezzanine at the height where neighbours have two or three. That is the ghetto's crowding, visible in the facade.

# Turin Concrete Map: Firsts, Science and Labour Sites (Category B, Run 2)

The strongest finds in Turin for a scientist's map are two 1808 obelisks. They still mark the ends of Giovanni Battista Beccaria's 18th-century geodetic baseline: one in Piazza Statuto, its twin 11,793.60 m (6,051.01 toises) west at Rivoli, per Carmelo Sena's Politecnico di Torino paper citing Delambre. Next to them are a chemistry plaque in Via Po marking the lab where Ascanio Sobrero first made nitroglycerine, and the 1890s anatomy, criminology and fruit-model museums in one building on Via Pietro Giuria. Turin's "firsts" are a mix. The 1896 Lumière screening in Via Po, the silent-film studio buildings and the Fiat factory at Corso Dante are well documented. The Juventus bench is a replica, the "first art-house cinema" is disputed, and most food firsts are marketing or tradition with nothing to see. For labour history, the sites with clear sources are the Gramsci lodging plaque and the L'Ordine Nuovo plaque. The places of 1943, 1969 and 1980 are spots on the street with no marker found.

## TL;DR
- **Best science stops:** the Beccaria obelisks (Piazza Statuto plus the Rivoli twin and its 1934 plaque); the Sobrero nitroglycerine plaque at Via Po 18/B; and the Palazzo degli Istituti Anatomici (Anatomy, Lombroso and Fruit museums, Mon–Sat 10–18). Add the 17th–19th-century pharmacies (Masino, Anglesio, Almasio), which still have original fittings.
- **Firsts with real buildings:** the ex-Ospizio di Carità at Via Po 33 (Lumière screening, 7 Nov 1896); the Ambrosio studio building at Via Mantova 34–38 (Fenoglio, 1911–13); Fiat's first plant at Corso Dante 102; and the Carpano vermouth plaque at Piazza Castello/Via Viotti. The Juventus bench (repainted July 2025) is only a commemorative stand-in, and Palazzo Bricherasio has no Fiat plaque.
- **Labour sites are thin on the ground:** Gramsci's 1957 plaque at Piazza Carlina 15 and the 1949 L'Ordine Nuovo plaque at Via Arcivescovado 7 are confirmed. Officina 19 (1943), Corso Traiano (1969) and the Teatro Nuovo (1980) have no plaque found. The search budget ran out before the mutual-aid society buildings could be checked.

## 1. The best 10
1. **Guglia Beccaria, Piazza Statuto.** A 7.94 m granite-and-bronze obelisk (1808), built on the stones Beccaria used as the Turin end of his geodetic baseline to Rivoli. The closest thing Turin has to Paris's standard-metre markers.
2. **Beccaria's twin obelisk and 1934 plaque, Rivoli.** The western end of the same baseline, plus a 1934 plaque set into the pavement by the newsstand at the start of Via Fratelli Piol. Standing at both ends lets you walk the measured line of Corso Francia.
3. **Sobrero plaque, Via Po 18/B.** "In the old chemical laboratory of this building, Ascanio Sobrero… first realising the synthesis of nitroglycerine." A chemist's pilgrimage spot, under the portico.
4. **Palazzo degli Istituti Anatomici, Via Pietro Giuria 15.** Three museums in one building: Rolando anatomy, the Lombroso criminal anthropology museum, and Garnier Valletti's fruit models.
5. **Ex-Ospizio di Carità, Via Po 33.** Vittorio Calcina's Lumière screening of about twenty shorts on 7 November 1896. Often called Italy's first public screening, but Rome contests that.
6. **Ambrosio studios, Via Mantova 34–38.** The office block and glass-roofed stage built by Pietro Fenoglio in 1911–13 for Italy's biggest silent-film studio still stand.
7. **Regia Farmacia Masino, Via Maria Vittoria 3.** Founded 1667; 18th-century fittings, original jars and a bronze mortar dated 1718; still trading.
8. **Casa Gramsci plaque, Piazza Carlina 15.** The 1957 plaque, "Here Antonio Gramsci lived in the years 1919–21", on what is now an NH hotel.
9. **Fiat's first plant, Corso Dante 102.** Built 1899–1900, centre of the September 1920 occupations, bombed 8 December 1942, now lofts.
10. **Carpano vermouth plaque, Piazza Castello at Via Viotti.** Records Carpano creating his vermouth "in this house" in 1786. The founding date is tradition but the shop location is well supported.

# Turin Concrete Map — Run 3: Odd Infrastructure, Odd Monuments, Urban Quirks

The best additions in these three themes are the surviving "Renzi" public urinals, the Liberty-style public bathhouses that still sell showers, the yellow 1912 toll houses on the old customs-wall squares, the icehouses inside the Porta Palazzo market hall, and the flood-height column by the Borgo Medievale. The famous rub-for-luck spots and "magic Turin" doors are real objects but mostly carry folklore.

## TL;DR
- **Infrastructure is the strongest theme.** About 29 historic "Renzi" urinals survive; Corriere Torino (Jan 2025) said the city wants to keep 13 "come elemento storico"; Piazza Villari and Piazza Sassari are the two Liberty-style survivors. Four municipal bathhouses (1900s–1950s) still work or were converted. Four 1912 toll houses still stand. Plus 19th-century icehouses in the Porta Palazzo market hall, a column recording 200 years of Po floods, and the rack tramway GTT bills as "unica nel suo genere in Italia".
- **Odd monuments are mostly well-known spots with wrong stories.** The lucky "Columbus finger" is a 1923 war memorial to emigrant volunteers; the "devil's door" is a real 1675 Parisian door with legendary ghosts; the Frejus "Lucifer" is a winged Genius of Science.
- **Urban quirks are thinner:** smallest piazzetta (~17 × <13 m), shortest street (via Ercole Ricotti, ~23–30 m), narrowest (vicolo Santa Maria, 2.85 m), and façade oddities: bats, dog heads, a bull bursting from a wall, an upside-down David.
